source: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (Asian disease, problems 1-2)
finding: Same outcomes worded as lives saved versus lives lost flip the choice between a sure option and a gamble. Sure option wins in the gain wording, gamble wins in the loss wording.
numbers: Problem 1 (N=152): Program A, 200 saved for sure, chosen by 72%; Program B, 1/3 chance all 600 saved, chosen by 28%. Problem 2 (N=155): Program C, 400 die for sure, 22%; Program D, 1/3 chance nobody dies, 78%. Between-subject, hypothetical.
limits: Single scenario, hypothetical, no incentives. The sure option is described incompletely (200 saved says nothing about the other 400), which later work shows matters.
agent_relevance: The agent should treat a changed answer after a pure wording flip as a defect to detect, not as a preference. This is the template test for paraphrase stability in S1.

source: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (concurrent decisions, problems 3-4)
finding: People who see two decisions separately are risk averse for the gain and risk seeking for the loss, and so pick a combination that is dominated by another combination they would take if it were written out as one option.
numbers: Problem 3 (N=150): sure gain $240 chosen by 84% over 25% chance of $1000; for losses, the gamble (75% chance to lose $1000) chosen by 87% over a sure loss of $750. Problem 4 (N=86): when the combined options are shown, 100% chose the dominant B&C and 0% the dominated A&D. Paid version (N=126, 1 in 10 played for real, outcomes scaled down by 50): 67% chose A, 86% chose D, dominated A&D chosen by 60%, dominant B&C by only 6%.
limits: Shows monetary incentives did not remove the effect. Authors say effects are large and systematic but not universal.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a fix that works: write the joint option out explicitly. An operator that recombines parts into one explicit statement before judging is supported.

source: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (pseudocertainty, problems 5-7)
finding: Framing a contingency as a two-stage game makes a probabilistic prize feel like a sure thing, and preferences reverse between logically equivalent versions.
numbers: Problem 5 (N=77): sure $30 78% vs 80% chance of $45 22%. Problem 6 (N=85, two-stage game, 25% chance to reach stage 2): C sure $30 74%, D 80% chance of $45 26%. Problem 7 (N=81): 25% chance of $30 42% vs 20% chance of $45 58%. Within-subject group (N=205): over 75% made compatible choices on problems 5 and 6; under half were compatible across 6 and 7 or 5 and 7.
limits: Within-subject data show the inconsistency exists inside one person, not only across groups.
agent_relevance: Equivalent descriptions of one probability structure can get different answers from the same judge. Use several equivalent restatements and compare them in code.

source: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (accounts and reference points, problems 8-10)
finding: How an outcome is booked (which account, which reference point) changes the choice even when money is identical.
numbers: Problem 8 (N=183): after losing a $10 bill, 88% still buy a $10 ticket. Problem 9 (N=200): after losing the $10 ticket itself, only 46% buy another. Problem 10 (N=93 and N=88): 68% would drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 calculator, only 29% to save $5 on a $125 calculator.
limits: Hypothetical questions, US-style prices of 1981.
agent_relevance: The same fact framed against a different baseline changes what the judge does. S1 restatement should state baselines explicitly.

source: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (theory and normative argument)
finding: Framing is the decision maker's own representation of acts, contingencies and outcomes. A reference point turns outcomes into gains or losses, and the value function is concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses. People usually do not notice alternative frames, want preferences to be frame independent, but often cannot resolve the conflict.
numbers: Examples: race-track bettor who has lost $140 treats the last bet as a way back to even; cash discount versus credit-card surcharge; calling a sure loss an insurance premium raises its acceptance.
limits: Authors say acting on the most readily available frame may be defended by mental effort cost, but prospect theory fits the details better. The normative claim (description invariance) was developed in Tversky and Kahneman (1986).
agent_relevance: Gives the design principle for S1: produce more than one frame and check the answer is invariant. Describes the failure of an agent that never looks for another frame.

source: Sher and McKenzie (2008) Framing effects (encyclopedia entry); typology after Levin, Schneider, Gaeth (1998)
finding: Three families of framing: attribute (one attribute, positive versus negative proportion), risky choice (sure thing versus gamble in gain or loss terms), goal (urging action by stressing gains of acting or losses of not acting). Attribute framing gives a valence-consistent shift: 75% lean beats 25% fat. Description invariance (Tversky and Kahneman 1986) is the norm being violated.
numbers: Examples cited: beef rated higher as 75% lean than 25% fat (Levin and Gaeth 1988); R&D teams get more funds when performance is framed as success (Duchon et al. 1989).
limits: Encyclopedia entry; numbers from the cited studies are not given here.
agent_relevance: Our subfield label ('25% fat' versus '75% lean') is attribute framing, the smallest effect type in the meta-analysis (see a07). Use it as the cheapest paraphrase-stability test.

source: Pinon and Gambara (2005) A meta-analytic review of framing effect: risky, attribute and goal framing
finding: Framing effects are small to moderate and heterogeneous. Risky and goal framing are about equal, attribute framing is smaller.
numbers: 51 studies (1997-2003), 151 effect sizes, nearly 13,500 subjects. d = 0.437 risky, 0.260 attribute, 0.444 goal. Heterogeneity significant (p<.0001). Asian disease was 47.7% of tasks, d = 0.43. Attribute framing: student samples d=0.22, between-subjects d=0.24, single option d=0.19 vs multiple options d=0.37.
limits: Covers only 1997-2003. Self-selected literature, no correction for publication bias. Effect sizes vary with response mode, domain and design.
agent_relevance: A wording shift moves human answers by about 0.3 to 0.45 SD on average. This is the human yardstick for the agent.

source: Kuhberger (2023) A systematic review of risky-choice framing effects (EXCLI Journal)
finding: Risky-choice framing is robust across meta-analyses and large replications at about d = 0.5 to 0.6 once publication bias is checked, but there is no single true effect size.
numbers: Kuhberger (1998): over 100 studies, over 200 effect sizes, about 30,000 participants, weighted d = 0.31. Steiger and Kuhberger (2018) bias-corrected d = 0.52; 2016-only studies d = 0.56. Many Labs 1 (Klein et al. 2014) d = 0.60. Im and Chen (2022): Cohen's h = 0.612, 95% CI [0.568, 0.656], over 100,000 participants, 49 countries. Range across task variants d = 0.16 to 0.91. d = 0.60 equals moving success from 36% to 64% (binomial effect size display).
limits: Secondary report of the original meta-analyses and of Many Labs 1; I did not open those primary papers. Many Labs 1 figure is as quoted by this review.
agent_relevance: A realistic target for how large a wording effect should look in a human-like model. Task variants change the effect a lot, so test with many variants.

source: Kuhberger (2023) systematic review: ADP variants and generalisation
finding: In Asian-disease-like tasks the sure option is chosen far more often in gain wording. The effect generalises across many facets.
numbers: Kuhberger et al. (1999) meta-analysis, over 40 studies: 63% chose the sure option as a gain, 41% as a loss (difference 22 points). DeKay et al. (2022) metastudy varied domain (lives, money, animals, crops), magnitude (x0.1 to x10), 13 probabilities, probability format, order, layout: average effect about 26 percentage points, generalised over almost all facets.
limits: Second-hand report of both studies. Cumulative prospect theory predicts a reversal at low probabilities; the 1999 meta-analysis found no such reversal.
agent_relevance: A paraphrase test suite can vary the same facets (domain, numbers, order, format) and expect the human-like effect everywhere; the agent should be invariant to all of them.

source: Kuhberger (2023) systematic review: moderators and non-risky framing
finding: Individual differences barely predict susceptibility. Message (goal) framing is weak. Attribute framing on food moves attitudes a lot but intentions hardly at all.
numbers: No consistent link with thinking styles (Wyszynski and Diederich 2023), numeracy small (Peters and Levin 2008), age small (Best and Charness 2015, 18 studies, over 3,000 people). Message framing about d = 0.10 (O'Keefe and Jensen 2008, 2009). Food attribute framing (Dolgopolova et al. 2021): 25 studies, 76 effect sizes, d = 0.47 overall, d = 0.82 attitudes, d = 0.05 intentions. Forced deliberation shrinks the effect in some studies (Almashat 2008).
limits: Review summary, not primary data.
agent_relevance: Wording shifts evaluations more than actions. Judge-type outputs (ratings) are more at risk than final decisions that are checked.

source: Kuhberger (2023) systematic review: theories (prospect theory, motivation, fuzzy-trace, communication)
finding: Four families of explanation. Cumulative prospect theory: value function plus decision weights. Motivational: security versus potential, regulatory focus. Fuzzy-trace theory: gist ('some saved' beats 'some saved or none'). Communicative: the sure option is described incompletely, so listeners infer the rest.
numbers: Value function parameters (Tversky and Kahneman 1992): alpha = beta = 0.88, lambda = 2.25. Loss aversion meta-analysis (Brown et al. 2021): over 600 estimates, mean lambda = 1.955. Venture theory (Hogarth and Einhorn 1990) and the Advantage model (Shafir et al. 1993) are alternative formal models. Kuhberger and Gradl (2013): framing changes the evaluation of the riskless option but hardly the risky one.
limits: No single theory explains all variants. Cognitive-formal models fit curves but do not explain where the curve shape comes from.
agent_relevance: If the effect comes from an incompletely described sure option, then S1 should complete every option (state the complement) before choosing. This is a testable, cheap operator.

source: Mandel (2014) Do framing effects reveal irrational choice? (as reported by secondary sources)
finding: Classic framing effect depends on whether people read the sure-option quantifier as 'exactly' or 'at least'. Made explicit, the effect vanishes.
numbers: Three findings as summarised in secondary sources: exact wording made explicit removes the effect; 'at least' wording restores it; most people read the quantifiers as lower bounds.
limits: I did not open the paper. Taken from a search summary and the Kuhberger review's description.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: some of the human effect is rational inference from ambiguous wording. An S1 restatement that disambiguates quantifiers would remove it.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2 (replication of Tversky and Kahneman 1981 Study 10, mental accounting)
finding: Many Labs 2 replicated the jacket/calculator account-framing problem (not the Asian disease problem). The effect replicated, at about half the original size.
numbers: Original: 181 people, 68% vs 29% would travel to save $5, OR = 4.96. Replication aggregate N = 7,228: 49% (cheap item on sale) vs 32% (costly item), d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.35, 0.45], OR = 2.06 [1.87, 2.27]. Heterogeneity across sites: tau = 0.00, Q(54) = 55.20, p = 0.43, I-squared 6%.
limits: This is not the gain-loss Asian disease item. Items were re-priced and re-worded for 2014 with an original author's help. The Asian disease replication was in Many Labs 1 (not opened).
agent_relevance: A classic framing finding survives a large cross-site replication at reduced size with almost no site heterogeneity: a stable target for a test suite.

source: Slovic (1995) The construction of preference (response-mode reversals)
finding: Preferences are often constructed during elicitation, not read from a stored list. Choices and prices of the same gambles disagree systematically.
numbers: Lichtenstein and Slovic (1973, Las Vegas casino): P bet (11/12 to win 12 chips) and $ bet (2/12 to win 79 chips) chosen about equally often, yet the $ bet got the higher selling price about 88% of the time; of people who chose the P bet, 87% priced the $ bet higher. Slovic and Lichtenstein (1968): ratings and choices follow probabilities, prices follow dollar amounts.
quote: preferences are often constructed--not merely revealed--in the process of elicitation
limits: Review of work from 1968 to 1995. Small-stakes gambles; some economists argued incentives and markets shrink reversals, but Grether and Plott (1979) and others found they persist.
agent_relevance: Different readouts of the same belief (choose, rate, price, rank) can disagree. For the agent: ask for one fixed readout format, and never mix scores from different formats.

source: Slovic (1995) The construction of preference (causes: compatibility, prominence)
finding: Reversals are mostly violations of procedure invariance, not intransitivity. The compatibility hypothesis says an attribute counts more when it matches the response scale (prices pull toward dollar amounts). The prominence hypothesis says the more important attribute counts more in choice than in matching.
numbers: Tversky, Slovic and Kahneman (1990): reversal rate 40 to 50%; only about 10% of reversal patterns intransitive, about 90% violated procedure invariance; overpricing of the low-probability bet explained nearly two thirds. Highway safety problem: 67% chose the program saving more lives. Irwin et al. (1993): 41% reversed between choosing clean air and pricing a computer upgrade higher.
limits: Mechanism explanations are post hoc and several remain contested.
agent_relevance: Weighting of attributes depends on the answer format. A scaffold that extracts a score and a choice separately should check they agree.

source: Slovic (1995) The construction of preference (adaptive decision maker)
finding: Payne, Bettman and Johnson's adaptive decision maker builds a strategy on the spot, sensitive to task complexity, time pressure, response mode and framing. Construction tactics: anchoring and adjustment, leaning on the prominent dimension, dropping common elements, adding attributes to make one option dominate.
numbers: No new numbers; synthesis of Payne, Bettman and Johnson (1992, 1993), Shafir, Simonson and Tversky (1993), Montgomery (1983) dominance search.
limits: I did not open Payne, Bettman and Johnson (1992, 1993) themselves; this is Slovic's description of them.
agent_relevance: Models the human judge as a strategy picker with effort-accuracy trade-offs. Supports G12 (spend by difficulty) and warns that a judge LLM may be building its answer from the readily available cue.

source: Leong, McKenzie, Sher, Muller-Trede (2017) The role of inference in attribute framing effects
finding: Attribute framing works largely through inference: listeners treat the chosen frame as a hint about what is typical. Passing these inferred values to people who never saw the frame produces a framing effect anyway.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=414): basketball player described as 'made' versus 'missed' free throws: ratings 4.93 vs 3.42, t(136)=4.75, d = 0.81. Yoked recipients, who only saw the inferred typical value, still showed d = 0.40. Correlation between inferred typical value and recipient rating r(128) = -.767. Exp 2 (N=364): framing effect at zero quiz score b = 2.27, shrinking with knowledge, interaction b = -0.28, t(360) = -2.10.
limits: Single domains (basketball, medical); effect shrinks but does not vanish with expertise.
agent_relevance: A neutral restatement should strip the speaker's frame and also the hidden reference point. Prior knowledge of the attribute's base rate reduces susceptibility; give the agent the base rate.

source: McKenzie and Nelson (2003) What a speaker's choice of frame reveals (as reported by secondary sources)
finding: Speakers pick the frame that matches their reference point, and listeners decode it. A half-full glass is more often called 'half full' if it was previously empty.
numbers: No numbers recorded here.
limits: Seen only through citations in Sher and McKenzie and a search summary; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that logically equivalent frames carry different information. A paraphrase that is logically equivalent is not necessarily information equivalent.

source: Levin, Schneider, Gaeth (1998) All frames are not created equal (as reported by secondary sources)
finding: Typology of framing: risky choice, attribute and goal framing, argued to tap different processes, which explains conflicting results across studies.
numbers: OBHDP 76(2), 149-188. No numbers recorded.
limits: I only saw the abstract and citations in other sources; not opened.
agent_relevance: Reminds us to test each framing type separately; do not generalise from one task.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases (GPT-3 framing)
finding: GPT-3 davinci-002 largely reproduces the Tversky and Kahneman pattern near the original probability (1/3): it rarely picks the risky option in save wording and more often in die wording. At higher save probabilities it picks the risky option in both.
numbers: Mean risky-choice rate over save probabilities 1/6 to 5/6: save framing 45.4%, die framing 74.1% (human: 28% and 78%). Save probability below 0.5: 11.3% vs 60.0%; at 0.5: 21.9% vs 46.9%; above 0.5: 84.4% vs 93.8%.
limits: Base GPT-3, 600-person scenario, prompt in the original format with 'Answer: Option'. Only one model. No variance across paraphrases.
agent_relevance: Wording shifts a base model's choice by a human-sized amount near the classic setting. The effect disappears (both wordings risky) when the probability is far from the classic value, so test near the classic regime.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) (irrelevant-context 'framing' of code prompts)
finding: A different use of the word framing: putting irrelevant functions plus a bait line before a coding prompt makes code models copy the bait line.
numbers: HumanEval functional accuracy for Codex fell from 32.9% to between 2.4% and 10.6% with preceding irrelevant functions; CodeGen from 25.6% to between 1.5% and 11.0%. The bait line 'raise NotImplemented' was output verbatim 91.7% (Codex) and 79.3% (CodeGen) of the time after framing, versus 1.4% and 0.0% before.
limits: This is priming by irrelevant context, not equivalent wording. Do not mix it with wording-equivalence results.
agent_relevance: Distractor text in the prompt can capture the output; keep S1 restatements free of irrelevant context.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 reproduced three of six prospect-theory biases from Kahneman and Tversky (1979): a framing effect, a certainty effect and an overweighting of small-probability differences.
numbers: Replicated the original analysis with GPT-3 choice probabilities; three of six effects found (framing, certainty, overweighting). No sample size for framing alone in the main text.
limits: Only GPT-3 (davinci family); details are in the supplement, which I did not open.
agent_relevance: Framing sensitivity is present in an older model by default. Measure it again on the model we use.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT shows a clear framing effect on a medicine-efficacy rating, in the same direction as people.
numbers: Gain frame ('70 patients improved') vs loss frame ('30 did not'), 1-7 efficacy scale. ChatGPT: 5 in all 11 gain-frame runs, 4 in all 11 loss-frame runs. Humans (82 US workers; 44 gain, 39 loss): 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80) = 3.86, p < .001.
limits: 11 runs per condition, one prompt pair; ChatGPT answers were identical every run, so the effect is deterministic for that wording.
agent_relevance: A rating-style judge can be moved by '70 improved' versus '30 did not' wording. Judge prompts should use one canonical wording.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (framing, admissions)
finding: Asking 'would you admit this student' versus 'would you reject this student' changes the admission rate for the same student. GPT-4 shows the biggest swing.
numbers: Admission rate under the admit question vs the reject question: GPT-4 0.375 vs 0.780 (difference -0.405); GPT-3.5-turbo 0.685 vs 0.520 (+0.165); Llama-2-13b 0.002 vs 0.062; direction differs by model. Prompts built from a pool of student profiles; GPT runs limited to 400 prompts per experiment.
limits: One task type, admissions; sign of the effect differs by model; Llama-2 models are near floor so the comparison is weak.
agent_relevance: A bare yes/no wording flip can change a strong model's answer by about 40 points. Never use a negated or reversed question as the only readout.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (self-help rewrite)
finding: Letting the model rewrite the prompt to remove bias, then answering the rewritten prompt, removes the framing swing for GPT-4 almost fully. Few-shot fixes can break the model.
numbers: Selfhelp rewrite (one extra forward pass, prompt: 'Rewrite the following prompt such that a reviewer would not be biased by cognitive bias'): GPT-4 admission 0.270 vs 0.280 (difference -0.010; baseline -0.405); GPT-3.5-turbo 0.435 vs 0.515 (-0.080; baseline +0.165); Llama-2-13b 0.355 vs 0.311. Remaining biased framing prompts: 0% Llama-2-13b, 1.4% Llama-2-7b, 2.7% GPT-4. Contrastive few-shot made Llama-2-7b admit or reject about 100% of cases (0.996, 1.000).
limits: The rewritten prompt is a different text, so correctness was not measured, only consistency. One task. The rewrite alone is unsupervised.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S1 neutral restatement. Consistency is not accuracy, so the restatement must keep every fact. Check the restatement in code (same numbers, same entities).

source: Saeedi, Goodarzi, Canbaz (2024) Heuristics and biases in AI decision-making: implications for responsible AGI
finding: Models contradict themselves between positive and negative wording of the same scenario in most cases.
numbers: 1,500 experiments over nine biases. Contradictory responses to positive vs negative framing of identical scenarios: GPT-4o 57%, Gemma 2 74%, Llama 3.1 85%. Llama 3.1 refused to support the positive version of a scenario in over 44% of framing experiments; GPT-4o supported a life-saving drug that 'diminishes 500 members' in 43% of runs.
limits: Output labelled as support or not support, a looser task than a forced choice. Default temperature. Contradiction rate counts any mismatch, no chance baseline.
agent_relevance: Even recent models contradict across wording often on this test. The scaffold needs paraphrase stability as a measured gate, not an assumption.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Framing effect is the fourth strongest of 30 biases and shows up in every one of 20 models tested.
numbers: 30,000 test cases, 30 biases, 20 models. Framing-effect bias score averaged 0.41 across models (random baseline 0.01), range 0.10 to 0.55 across models. Anchoring averaged 0.39, loss aversion 0.33, information bias 0.54, in-group bias 0.41.
limits: Scores are absolute bias magnitudes from a template framework with generated scenarios, not human effect sizes, so they cannot be compared directly with d values.
agent_relevance: Large, cheap benchmark that includes a framing test; useful source of test items for our paraphrase-stability harness.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in large language models
finding: Five LLMs, including reasoning models, show gain/loss framing effects, but size and even direction depend on the scenario. Sports and some geopolitical scenarios give very large effects; business and some others small or reversed.
numbers: 2,550 decisions (5 models, 25 iterations per condition; 750 civilian, 1,000 military, 400 mathematical). Championship strategy: loss frame chose BLITZ 85.6% vs gain frame 0.8%; framing effect +1.64 (o3) and +1.80 (Claude-4) on a risk score. Career transition: loss frame APPLY 87.2% vs gain 41.6%, effect -0.48 (o3). Business merger: p = 0.40 (o3), 0.31 (Claude-4), 0.40 (Gemini-1.5-Pro).
limits: Author's own scenarios, a single preprint; no human comparison group. The author notes Mandel (2014, 2015) showing classic effects shrink once quantifier interpretation is accounted for.
agent_relevance: Frame effects in current reasoning models are not removed by reasoning; they depend on context words. Test across domains, including loaded domains.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design
finding: Meaning-preserving changes in prompt format change accuracy a lot, and bigger models, more examples or instruction tuning do not remove the effect.
numbers: Spread up to 76 accuracy points for LLaMA-2-13B between equivalent formats; about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks. GPT-3.5: median spread 6.4 points, up to 56 points, over 320 formats and 53 tasks (under 10 USD per task using FormatSpread).
limits: Formatting (separators, casing, spacing), not framing of content. Few-shot, mostly classification tasks.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap way to measure paraphrase stability: report spread over many equivalent formats, not a single prompt. Supports G7 (cost counted).
